{{nihongo|'''Hotel Okura Tokyo'''|ホテルオークラ東京|Hoteru Ōkura Tōkyō}} is a luxury hotel opened in 1962 in [[Minato, Tokyo|Minato]], [[Tokyo]], Japan. It is operated by [[Okura Hotels]] and is a member of [[The Leading Hotels of the World]]. The historic main wing was demolished in 2015, with a modern replacement on the site opening in 2019, rebranded as '''The Okura Tokyo'''.<ref name="article100586">{{cite web|url=https://www.hotelnewsresource.com/article100586.html|title=Hotel Okura Tokyo Rebrands as the Okura Tokyo|website=Hotel News Resource|access-date=18 July 2025}}</ref>

The Hotel Okura Tokyo (now The Okura Tokyo), the [[Imperial Hotel, Tokyo]], and the [[Hotel New Otani Tokyo]], are often referred to as one of the {{nihongo|Three Great Hotels|御三家|[[gosanke]]}} of Tokyo, in a reference to the three [[Edo period|Edo-era]] branch houses of the [[Tokugawa clan]].

The hotel grounds also host the [[Okura Museum of Art]], which houses a collection of Japanese and East Asian art amassed by industrialist [[Okura Kihachiro|Ōkura Kihachirō]].

== History ==
=== First building (1962–2015) ===
Designed by [[Yoshiro Taniguchi]], the historic 408-room Main Wing opened on 20 May 1962. The 388-room South Wing opened on 26 November 1973.<ref name="history"/> The hotel is located near [[Embassy of the United States, Tokyo|the United States Embassy]] in the [[Akasaka, Tokyo|Akasaka]] area, and hosted every [[President of the United States]] since [[Richard Nixon]], as well as numerous other foreign heads of state.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.hotelokura.co.jp/tokyo/special/50th_anniversary/history/history4.html|title=ホテルオークラ東京50年のあゆみ 世界のVIPとホテルオークラ東京|website=Hotel Okura Tokyo|language=ja|access-date=18 July 2025}}</ref> The South Wing can be cut off from the rest of the building to serve as lodging for reporters and logistics aides, while using the penthouse "Imperial Suite" as high-security VIP lodging.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.enpitu.ne.jp/usr6/bin/day?id=60769&pg=20120829|title=活字中毒R.|website=Enpitu.ne.jp|language=ja|access-date=18 July 2025}}</ref>

The hotel became a member of Pan Am's [[InterContinental|Intercontinental Hotels]] division on 1 June 1964,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://digitalcollections.library.miami.edu/digital/collection/asm0341/id/120661/rec/166|title=Page 31|website=University of Miami Digital Collections|access-date=18 July 2025}}</ref> and would remain part of the chain until 1972, though it was never branded as an Intercontinental. The hotel has appeared in novels such as ''[[1Q84]]'' by [[Haruki Murakami]], and ''[[The Ninja (novel)|The Ninja]]'' by [[Eric Van Lustbader]]. In [[Ian Fleming]]'s novel ''[[You Only Live Twice (novel)|You Only Live Twice]]'', James Bond stays at the Okura while in Tokyo. In the movie ''[[Walk, Don't Run (film)|Walk, Don't Run]]'', Sir William Rutland ([[Cary Grant]]) tries to check in at the fully-booked Okura two days before the 1964 Olympics in Tokyo.

The hotel has also been the site of several major international summits, and has also provided catering to international summits held off-site.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.hotelokura.co.jp/tokyo/special/50th_anniversary/history/history3.html|title=ホテルオークラ東京50年のあゆみ 世界をもてなすホテルオークラ東京|website=Hotel Okura Tokyo|language=ja|access-date=18 July 2025}}</ref> In 1976, [[JVC]] chose the Okura Hotel for the launch of the [[JVC HR-3300|world's first VHS videocassette recorder]].

The original Main Wing closed in August 2015 for demolition, leaving only the smaller South Tower operating. The demolition plans were met with dismay by travel journalists, like [[Tyler Brûlé]], who called the original "a masterpiece" and "one of the most loved modernist hotels in the world".<ref name="TB">{{cite news|url=http://www.ft.com/intl/cms/s/2/27daaa30-f868-11e3-815f-00144feabdc0.html|title=The Fast Lane: Let's Save a Masterpiece|newspaper=Financial Times|date=11 July 2014|first=Tyler|last=Brûlé|access-date=22 June 2015}}</ref> Others lamented the irony of the iconic building and its "Orchid Bar", a favourite meeting place for the foreign diplomats from the many embassies nearby, being demolished at a time when shows like ''[[Mad Men]]'' have made the modernistic style of the 1960s highly fashionable again.<ref name=FAS>{{cite news|last=Maak|first=Niklas|title=Rettet die Zukunft! Oder fahrt noch mal hin|newspaper=Frankfurter Allgemeine Sonntagszeitung|pages=69|language=de|date=14 June 2015}}</ref> The outcry helped raise awareness of the significance of the original design, and many interior elements of the lobby were painstakingly transferred to or recreated within the new building by Yoshio Taniguchi, the son of the original designer.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://designanthologymag.com/story/hotel-okura|title=The Iconic Hotel Okura Reopens in Tokyo|last=Demetriou|first=Danielle|website=Design Anthology|access-date=1 December 2019}}</ref>

=== Second building (2019–present) ===
Following a ¥110 billion (US$1 billion) construction project, the hotel opened two new towers, with a total of 508 rooms, on 12 September 2019,<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/features/2019-09-12/okura-tokyo-hotel-reopens-after-1-billion-makeover-photos|title=Tokyo's Mid-Century Modern Icon is Back|newspaper=Bloomberg.com|date=12 September 2019|access-date=18 July 2025}}</ref> in anticipation of the [[2020 Tokyo Olympics]]. The Okura Prestige Tower is a {{cvt|188|m}} tall, 41-storey mixed-use tower with 368 modern international hotel rooms and 18 storeys of office space.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.hotelnewsresource.com/article78125.html|title=Hotel Okura Tokyo US$980 Million Reconstruction Begins in 2015|website=Hotel News Resource|access-date=18 July 2025}}</ref> The Okura Heritage Tower is an adjacent 75-metre, 17-storey tower offering 140 traditional Japanese guest rooms.<ref name="article100586" /> The complex was designed and built by [[Taisei Corporation]].<ref>{{cite web|title=The Okura Prestige Tower|url=https://www.skyscrapercenter.com/building/the-okura-prestige-tower/21232|website=[[Council on Tall Buildings and Urban Habitat]]|access-date=18 July 2025}}</ref>

About half of the site is open to the public as a green area and plaza.<ref>{{cite web|last=Abdel|first=Hana|title=The Okura Tokyo / Taniguchi and Associates + TAISEI DESIGN Planners Architects & Engineers|url=https://www.archdaily.com/986584/the-okura-hotel-tokyo-taisei-design-planners-architects-and-engineers|website=ArchDaily|access-date=17 July 2022}}</ref>

=== South Wing ===
The Hotel Okura's South Wing opened on 26 November 1973, built in a style similar to the 1962 main building.<ref name="history"/> The 13-storey building was demolished between 2021–2022.<ref name="JPC">{{cite web|last=Ward|first=Zoe|date=15 November 2021|title=Demolition of Hotel Okura South Wing to Start Today|url=https://japanpropertycentral.com/2021/11/demolition-of-hotel-okura-south-wing-to-start-today/|website=Japan Property Central|access-date=17 July 2023}}</ref> Two buildings, a {{cvt|180|m}} tall 43-storey apartment tower, and a {{cvt|115|m}} tall 21-storey office tower, are currently planned for the site.<ref name="JPC"/>
